intro: Kanchanaburi is a province that holds everything at once — emerald waterfalls, an iron bridge with a history behind it, and a riverside you could spend the whole day on. We picked the 10 spots most visitors here never skip, from landmarks right in town to the waterfalls and Mon community that require a longer drive. Every card comes with coordinates, entry fees, and directions so you can plan one trip and cover everything.
chips: 🛕 Wat Tham Suea on the hill

blocks.html:
If you had to describe Kanchanaburi in a few words, it's a province that holds many different moods at once. The riverside town has an old iron bridge, a glass skywalk, and a night market you can walk and eat your way through all evening. Drive toward Si Sawat or Sai Yok and you get big waterfalls and deep forest. Anyone willing to make the long drive to Sangkhlaburi gets a Mon community and early-morning mist rolling over the water — a sight hard to find anywhere else. The beauty here is that you can travel many different ways in one province: wake up early for a waterfall, stop at a hilltop temple at midday, stroll the riverside as the sun goes down.

Many places on this list are names people have known for years. The Bridge over the River Kwai still has the historic railway running across it every day, and the River Kwai Bridge Week comes every year in late November to early December. Erawan Falls is a 7-tier limestone waterfall in Erawan National Park, famous for its emerald-green water. Wat Tham Suea has a large golden Buddha statue gleaming on the hillside above wide rice fields. Hellfire Pass Museum tells the story of the Death Railway from the Second World War in detail — and entry is free. All together, these are 10 places worth seeing with your own eyes.

blocks.name: Bridge over the River Kwai
blocks.signature: Walk across the historic iron bridge, watch the Death Railway train roll past, great sunset light in the evening
blocks.descHtml:
The Bridge over the River Kwai is Kanchanaburi's true landmark — a historic iron bridge built during the Second World War along the Death Railway route. It's open for walking across at any time, free of charge, and works well for history lovers, photographers, and families who want to bring older children to experience real history outside a classroom. The bridge stretches about 300 meters; walk across the steel walkway and you can look down at the Khwae Yai River flowing below.

The unmissable highlight is timing your visit for when the actual train crosses the bridge. There are alcoves spaced along the sides where you can duck as the train approaches — you stand there and watch the locomotive creep slowly past, close enough to almost touch. Reviews consistently say to check the train schedule in advance so you can position yourself for the shot of the train on the bridge. Another favorite moment: late afternoon as the sun goes down, golden light reflecting off the water, photographs come out beautiful with almost no editing needed.

The atmosphere midday can be intense — strong sun and big crowds, especially during high season and long weekends. Many Thai reviewers say that if you want the bridge to yourself, come before 7 AM. Around the bridge there are souvenir shops, restaurants, and riverside cafés to rest at. You can continue on foot to the Skywalk and the nearby market easily. Practical note: the bridge has minimal railings and some steel gaps underfoot — closed shoes make the walk more comfortable, and watch small children carefully.

Open approximately 06:00–19:00 daily. No entry fee, no advance booking required. Located in Tha Makham, Mueang Kanchanaburi, on the Khwae Yai River bank near the town center. Accessible by car or by taking the train and alighting at Saphan Kwai Yai station. Popular because it combines a top check-in spot, genuine historic value, and free all-day access — practically every Kanchanaburi trip starts here.
mustOrder: Walk the 300-meter iron bridge, take in the Khwae Yai River views
Watch the Death Railway train cross the bridge in slow motion
Photograph the golden light over the water at sunset
Browse souvenir shops and riverside cafés around the bridge
blocks.bestFor: Town landmark check-in, evening photography with golden light
blocks.zone: Tha Makham (Khwae Yai riverfront, near town center)

blocks.name: Erawan Falls (Erawan National Park)
blocks.signature: 7-tier limestone waterfall, emerald-green water, climb to upper tiers and swim with fish
blocks.descHtml:
If there's one waterfall everyone names first when Kanchanaburi comes up, it's Erawan Falls — a 7-tier limestone waterfall inside Erawan National Park. What draws people is the emerald-green water, its color coming from limestone minerals dissolved in the stream. On a bright day, sunlight piercing the pool makes the water look almost unreal. Great for families, couples, and anyone who wants to escape the heat and float in cool water surrounded by forest.

The highlight is climbing tier by tier. Tiers 1–3 have easy, partly paved trails — manageable with a stroller. Tiers 4–7 get steeper, with some scrambling and stairs, but they reward you: the upper tiers have fewer people and equally beautiful water. Don't miss getting into the water with the fish — they nibble at your legs gently, which many visitors find surprisingly fun. Reviews consistently name Tier 2 as the widest and most enjoyable for swimming. Tier 7, shaped roughly like the Erawan (three-headed elephant) that gives the falls its name, is the final destination — reaching the top takes about 1–1.5 hours.

Entry fee: Thai adults 60 THB, children 30 THB; foreign adults 300 THB; vehicles 30 THB. Good value for the scenery and the park's upkeep. Open daily 08:00–16:30, but the upper tiers usually stop admitting visitors before that closing time — going early gives you time to walk all tiers comfortably. Located in Tha Kradan, Si Sawat district, about 65 km from Kanchanaburi town; roughly 3 hours by car from Bangkok.

Important notes: no food or plastic bottles beyond Tier 2 (there are deposit and check-in points). Wear grippy shoes — the limestone is slippery. During the wet season the water may be murky and fast; the clearest water is from the end of the rainy season through the dry months. Highly popular year-round; on holidays and weekends, coming first thing in the morning makes a real difference.
mustOrder: Climb all 7 tiers of the emerald-green waterfall
Swim with the fish that nibble at your legs
Tier 2 — the widest pool, best for swimming
Tier 7 — the Erawan elephant-head formation
blocks.bestFor: Family waterfall trip — go early to walk all 7 tiers

blocks.name: Wat Tham Suea
blocks.signature: Large gold-mosaic Buddha, panoramic rice-field views from the hilltop, great photography spot
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Tham Suea is a hilltop temple set in the middle of rice fields in Muang Chum subdistrict, Tha Muang district, not far from Kanchanaburi town. It's a landmark visible from a distance — the golden Buddha gleaming on the summit stands out across the valley. A great fit for those who want to make merit, photographers after wide-open views, and families looking for a half-day trip from Bangkok. The star is the "Luang Pho Chin Prathan Phon" Buddha — a large blessing-posture statue, 9 soms and 9 inches tall, gilded all over, visible before you even start climbing.

The unmissable experience is climbing to the hilltop viewpoint. Reviews consistently say the view of the wide green rice fields, with the Mae Klong River and the mountain range as a backdrop, photographs beautifully from every angle. Another highlight: the eight-sided Ket Kaew Maha Prasat chedi, 69 meters tall in orange, where you can climb inside to venerate Buddha relics. Before harvest season when the paddies are still green, the views are especially striking — a favorite spot for photographers.

Getting up the hill: those who are fit can take the naga staircase (steep and narrow — be prepared). Otherwise, an electric tram runs for around 10–20 THB per person — much easier. Entry is free; you only pay for the tram and any merit-making offerings. Open daily; Mon–Fri approximately 07:30–16:30, Sat–Sun slightly earlier opening until later evening.

Popular because it combines genuine spiritual significance, beautiful architecture, and natural views all in one place. Consistently high review scores from both Thai and international visitors. Practical notes: midday sun and heat can be intense — bring a hat or umbrella. Dress modestly (covered shoulders and knees) as this is a working temple, and come in the morning or late afternoon for cooler conditions and better photography light.
mustOrder: Luang Pho Chin Prathan Phon — large golden Buddha
Hilltop viewpoint over the rice fields and Mae Klong River
Ket Kaew Maha Prasat chedi — 8-sided, 69 m tall
Ride the electric tram up the hill
blocks.bestFor: Merit-making + rice-field views — morning or late afternoon

blocks.name: Mon Bridge (Uttamanusorn Bridge), Sangkhlaburi
blocks.signature: Thailand's longest wooden bridge, walk it to experience Mon village life, winter mornings bring mist drifting over the water
blocks.descHtml:
The Mon Bridge — officially named Uttamanusorn Bridge — is the longest wooden bridge in Thailand, spanning the reservoir of Vajiralongkorn Dam to connect the town side with the Mon community of Ban Wang Ka. Its 800-plus meters of length exist because of the faith of Luang Pho Uttama, who led the Mon people to build it by hand. This is a place to walk slowly and absorb real daily life, not just pose for photos. Suitable for nature lovers, cultural travelers, couples, and families alike.

The unmissable moment is early morning, especially in winter when mist floats over the water, the morning light is soft, and Mon residents in traditional sarongs walk the bridge to offer alms — an image reviewers consistently describe as the most moving thing they saw. Try getting up for alms-giving on the bridge at dawn, then crossing to the Mon side for the morning market, sampling local Mon snacks and foods. Anyone after photographs can rent traditional Mon dress from shops nearby.

Walking the bridge is free. Open all day, but the best atmosphere is from before dawn to around 9 AM. The bridge is in Sangkhlaburi district, Nong Lu subdistrict — a long drive from Kanchanaburi town, roughly 3.5 hours. Most people stay overnight in a floating raft house or riverside accommodation to catch the morning light.

Popular because it weaves the beauty of nature, Mon culture, and a story of faith together in a way few places can match. Google rating 4.6 from over 10,000 reviews. Practical notes: some wooden planks have gaps and the bridge gets crowded on holidays — wear comfortable walking shoes, be careful while photographing, and respect the community that still uses this bridge every day for real life.
mustOrder: Walk the bridge at dawn to watch the mist
Join the alms-giving ceremony on the bridge
Cross to the Mon market and village
Dress in Mon traditional costume for photos
blocks.bestFor: Winter mornings — alms-giving and mist watching

blocks.name: Song Khwae Skywalk (Riverside Skywalk, Kanchanaburi)
blocks.area: Pak Phraek / Ban Tai, Mueang Kanchanaburi
blocks.signature: Glass walkway extending over the river, views of the confluence where the two Kwae rivers meet
blocks.descHtml:
Song Khwae Skywalk — most people just call it the Kanchanaburi Skywalk — is a glass-floored walkway jutting out over the river in the middle of Kanchanaburi town. It sits about 12 meters above the water and extends roughly 150 meters. What makes it famous: the viewing angle where you can stand and watch the Khwae Yai and Khwae Noi rivers meet and flow on together as the Mae Klong. At certain water levels, the two rivers run different colors side by side — a clear two-tone river, visible with the naked eye. Great for photography, couples, families, and anyone who wants to try walking on glass with a panoramic city view below.

The unmissable moment is at the far end of the walkway where the full confluence is visible, along with floating raft houses, riverside restaurants, and the spires of nearby temples. Most reviews agree the best time is around 17:00–18:00 when the sun is softer, the breeze picks up, and the sunset comes out beautifully. Midday tends to be hot since it's fully exposed. First-timers who are nervous about heights find the initial step onto the glass a bit nerve-racking but settle into it quickly and enjoy looking straight down at the river.

Entry fee is around 60 THB per person, which includes fabric shoe covers required to protect the glass floor. Large bags go into lockers at the base. Both a lift and stairs are available. Each group is limited in number for safety. A full visit takes under an hour. Cash or PromptPay accepted.

Located on the riverside near Pak Phraek, Songkhwae Road, Ban Tai subdistrict, Mueang district — near the city pillar shrine and the Pak Phraek night walking street. Easy access, parking nearby. Open daily approximately 08:00–19:00 (may close earlier around 17:00 on some days — check ahead). Popular as a new town-center landmark with an easy walk, worthwhile views, and a smooth connection into the evening market.
mustOrder: The two-river confluence viewpoint (Khwae Yai + Khwae Noi meeting to form the Mae Klong)
Walk the glass floor 12 meters above the water
Sunset views 17:00–18:00
Panoramic view of the city, raft houses, and riverside temples
blocks.bestFor: Evening river views and sunset — ideal for couples, families, and photographers

blocks.name: Giant Chamchuri Tree
blocks.area: Ko Samrong, Mueang Kanchanaburi (Lat Ya area)
blocks.signature: A century-old rain tree with an enormous canopy — walk under it, photograph the whole spread from below
blocks.descHtml:
The Giant Chamchuri Tree — or Giant Acacia as it is sometimes called — is a natural landmark that practically everyone passing through Kanchanaburi wants to check off. The draw is a single tree over a hundred years old, with a trunk so wide that locals say it takes ten people with arms outstretched to circle it. Its canopy fans out roughly 50 meters across and 20 meters high. Step under it and look up at the branches weaving into a green ceiling, and you feel very small. Great for photographers, families with young children who want to run around, and anyone in search of a quiet, shady place to sit and catch the breeze.

The unmissable highlight is walking the wooden bridge built in a loop around the base of the tree — it protects the roots and gives you a full view of the tree from every angle without standing on bare soil. The most popular shot is standing underneath and framing the entire canopy. The tree has also become better known recently after appearing in a popular Thai horror film, drawing even more visitors. Around the grounds there are food stalls, drinks, coffee, and local produce — some days horses are available for photo-riding too. Reviews consistently praise the cleanliness, the shade, and the refreshing air.

Entry is free. Wide free parking lot. Toilets available. You only spend money on food or community goods if you choose to. Located in the Ban Kasikorram area, Ko Samrong subdistrict, Mueang Kanchanaburi — not far from town, drive across the river and head toward Lat Ya for about 10–15 km. Open daily from early morning to evening (approximately 06:00–18:00; stalls may open later).

Small tips: for soft, flattering light and fewer crowds, come early morning or late afternoon. If you arrive too close to sunset the stalls may be closing up. Avoid leaning hard against the base — it's an old tree that has been carefully maintained for a long time. A quick visit here pairs well with a stop at Wat Tham Suea or other Kanchanaburi attractions along the way.
mustOrder: Walk under the canopy and photograph the whole tree
Wooden bridge looping around the base of the trunk
Pick up local food and community products
Follow the filming location from the Thihyod horror film
blocks.bestFor: Photographers and check-in visitors — morning or late afternoon

blocks.name: Robinson Lifestyle Kanchanaburi
blocks.signature: Town's main mall — Tops, Uniqlo, SF Cinema, and a full dining zone all under one roof
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Kanchanaburi and want somewhere cool to escape the heat, grab a meal, catch a film, or pick up supplies all in one stop, Robinson Lifestyle Kanchanaburi is the town's main mall — the spot both locals and visitors consistently head for. Everything is under one roof: the Robinson department store, a Tops supermarket for groceries and souvenirs, Uniqlo and Super Sports for clothing, and SF Cinema on the second floor for evening showings. A solid pick for families, groups, or anyone who has had a full day driving around and wants air-conditioned downtime.

The Food Haven zone is the highlight — a large dining section with everything from snacks and coffee shops to full meals. International fast-food names like KFC, pizza, ice cream, and local restaurants sit alongside each other. One lap around covers all the options. For shoppers, there's Power Buy, B2S, OfficeMate, Mr.DIY, and several beauty and cosmetics brands. Recently renovated in 2026 under the theme "Kan Feel Good," bringing over 200 shops with a brighter, more open layout.

Free entry. Wide free parking available all day. You only pay for food and shopping. A typical meal in the food zone runs about 60–150 THB per person. Located on the Kanchanaburi bypass road, Pak Phraek subdistrict — easy to reach from town. Open daily 10:00–21:00. Reviews consistently praise cleanliness, strong air conditioning, ample parking, and a full range of everyday necessities.

Worth knowing: if you're after high-end fashion brands as found in Bangkok, this mall focuses on mid-range brands that locals actually use. Some reviews mention the absence of a taxi drop-off point out front — if you're not driving, arrange your ride home in advance. Overall, a reliable pit stop to recharge, buy snacks, and cool down between sightseeing in Kanchanaburi.
mustOrder: Food Haven zone — full dining selection
SF Cinema on the 2nd floor
Buy souvenirs at Tops
Shop at Uniqlo
blocks.bestFor: Eat, shop, and catch a film all in one place — good for families

blocks.name: Ploen Kan Market
blocks.signature: Riverside night market with a giant Ferris wheel, plenty of food, and live music
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Kanchanaburi and want a relaxed evening out, Ploen Kan Market is where locals point you. It's a riverside night market in the Tha Makham area, Mueang Kanchanaburi — open not long and already a new landmark people talk about. The first thing you notice is a large, colorful Ferris wheel lit up at night along the riverfront. It's the photo-spot everyone grabs, and after dark it looks genuinely impressive. Works equally well for couples, families, or groups.

The food selection is substantial — restaurants, desserts, drinks, and handmade goods, all at local market prices. Many reviews highlight the live music played every evening; sitting with something to eat, listening to songs with the river breeze, is the real draw. There's also a playground zone so kids can run around and parents can relax. A yellow rabbit sculpture and a performance stage add to the photo-spot count. The overall feel is green and airy with plenty of seating, both riverside and in the middle of the market.

Free entry, free parking, so there's no real planning needed — just drive up and walk in. Open daily (closed Tuesdays) from 17:00 to midnight. Located on the Tha Makham riverside, Mahadthai Road, close to the town center. Popular because it packages everything a night-out crowd wants: good food, a walk, great photos, and entertainment for all ages.

Small notes: weekends get notably busy. If you want a more relaxed experience, weekday evenings before the peak hours are ideal. Check the market's page ahead in case of special events or performances. Once you arrive, head for the Ferris wheel at night for views of the lit-up riverside — well worth the ride.
mustOrder: Ride the giant riverside Ferris wheel after dark
Sit by the river listening to live music
Graze through the street-food stalls
Photograph the yellow rabbit and the lights
blocks.bestFor: Riverside dinner, couples and families, chill evening stroll

blocks.name: Death Railway — Tham Krasae Curve
blocks.signature: Ride the train slowly across a wooden trestle clinging to the cliff face, with the Khwae Noi River flowing far below
blocks.descHtml:
If there's one spot in Kanchanaburi that deserves a slow visit, it's the Death Railway at the Tham Krasae curve. This wooden trestle runs about 400 meters along the cliff face above the Khwae Noi River — part of the Thai-Burma railway built during the Second World War using POW and forced labor, at enormous human cost. This particular stretch was the most difficult and dangerous to construct, earning the name "Death Curve." Great for history enthusiasts, photographers, and anyone who wants a genuine vintage-train experience in a mountain river valley.

The highlight is riding the train as it creeps across the wooden trestle on the curve — the wheels clicking over the sleepers, wide river views opening out the windows, everyone reaching for their cameras at the same moment. Nearby is Tham Krasae Cave, with a Buddha image inside that was once a shelter for POWs. A short walk from the end of the bridge brings you there. The area overall is quiet, shaded, and breezy from the river — there are small souvenir shops and food stalls around.

Walking the bridge and entering the cave is free. If you want the full experience, buy a train ticket to ride across — around 100 THB for foreigners, less for Thais. The site is about 15 km from Kanchanaburi town. You can drive or take the Namtok–Kanchanaburi train and alight at the Tham Krasae stop. The area is open daily approximately 07:00–17:00; the train passes 6 times a day, outbound trains around 07:36, 11:51, and 17:50. Check the schedule before going so you time it right.

Worth knowing: the bridge is still active railway. When walking on it, stay alert — if you hear a train coming, move immediately to one of the safety alcoves. Visitors with a fear of heights may feel uneasy since you can see right through the wooden gaps to the river below. During train-crossing times and long holidays the bridge gets very crowded. For quieter conditions and better light, aim for late afternoon around 16:00–17:00.
mustOrder: Ride the train across the Tham Krasae trestle curve
Walk the wooden bridge along the cliff face
Pay respects at the Buddha image in Tham Krasae Cave
blocks.bestFor: History lovers, photographers, scenic train ride
blocks.hours: Open daily 07:00–17:00. Train passes 6 times daily (outbound approx. 07:36, 11:51, 17:50)

blocks.name: Hellfire Pass Museum (Chong Khao Khat)
blocks.signature: Walk the Death Railway cut made by hand through a mountain — museum tells the WWII story
blocks.descHtml:
If there's one place in Kanchanaburi that rewards taking it slowly, it's Hellfire Pass Museum — called Chong Khao Khat in Thai. This is the point on the Death Railway where Second World War POWs carved through solid rock by hand, with almost no tools and little food; many died here. The museum tells the story through exhibits, authentic POW personal items, a reconstructed camp life room, and a short documentary that many reviews recommend watching before walking the trail. Excellent for history lovers, families, and anyone who wants a trip with genuine weight to it.

The unmissable experience is walking the railway trail down to the actual cutting — rock walls over ten meters high on both sides, shaped entirely by human hands. The path descends wooden stairs and a ramp to a comfortable packed-earth trail. Numbered stopping points along the way let you play the free audio guide, which tells stories in the words of real survivors. You can walk just to the cutting or go the full route — about 3–4 hours. Many foreign reviewers say they walked back in tears, thinking about the people who died here.

Entry is completely free — both the museum and the trail. There is a donation box for those who want to contribute to the site's upkeep. Signage is in both Thai and English. The air-conditioned exhibit hall is comfortable and well maintained. The site is managed by the Australian Army's veterans affairs department, which keeps the presentation at a very high standard. Located in Tha Sao, Sai Yok, northwest of Kanchanaburi town — a car is the most convenient way to get there. Open daily 09:00–16:00.

What makes people talk about this place is that it isn't a walk-through museum — it's a site where you stand at the actual location, hear the actual voices, and feel it for yourself. Practical notes: you need to collect a visitor pass at the entrance gate since it's within a military compound. Go in the morning to avoid the afternoon heat. Wear comfortable walking shoes and bring water, because the return is uphill.
mustOrder: Stand inside the hand-cut railway pass
Listen to the audio guide narrated by real survivors
Watch the short documentary before descending the trail
View authentic exhibits and the reconstructed POW camp room
blocks.bestFor: History lovers, families — visit in the morning

blocks.title: What to know before visiting Kanchanaburi

items.title: Drive yourself — it's by far the easiest
items.text: Kanchanaburi's attractions are spread out and public transport is limited. Renting or driving your own car is the most flexible option. Within the town center you can call Grab, but heading to the waterfalls or Sangkhlaburi really requires your own wheels.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Waterfall entry fees, the temple tram, and many night market stalls are cash-only. Keep small bills handy — even if big malls like Robinson accept cards and QR payments.

items.title: Go early to avoid the crowds
items.text: Erawan Falls and Wat Tham Suea get packed from mid-morning, especially on holidays. Going right when they open means a comfortable walk and much better photos. Mon Bridge is most beautiful in winter morning mist.

items.title: Dress modestly for temples
items.text: Wat Tham Suea is a sacred site. Dress with covered shoulders and knees, remove shoes at the marked points, and move with the same respect you'd see from other visitors.

items.title: English is adequate at major sites
items.text: Top landmarks and Hellfire Pass Museum have English-language signs. Local markets and smaller shops may have limited English — a translation app works well for ordering food or asking directions.

items.title: Wear shoes you can walk in
items.text: Erawan Falls requires walking slippery limestone on the way to upper tiers. Wat Tham Suea has many stairs. Hellfire Pass has a trail following the railway route. Trainers or hiking shoes are far better than sandals.

blocks.title: Plan your Kanchanaburi trip to get the most out of one visit
blocks.html:
To cover the most ground in one day, organize by zone. Start early and drive directly to Erawan Falls — it gets crowded quickly, and hiking all the tiers takes time. On the way back, stop at Wat Tham Suea in Tha Muang — the electric tram up costs 10 THB and saves the 158 naga-staircase steps if you're not up for the climb. Late afternoon, knock off the town landmarks in one go: the Bridge over the River Kwai at golden hour is ideal for photos, then continue to Song Khwae Skywalk to see the two-river confluence, and close the day at Ploen Kan Market or the Pak Phraek riverfront walking street.

Mon Bridge in Sangkhlaburi and Hellfire Pass Museum in Sai Yok are in opposite directions and each takes a half-day at minimum. Keep them for separate days. Sangkhlaburi is about 3–4 hours from town by car — if you want the morning mist at the bridge, staying overnight locally is the smart move. Hellfire Pass is free, with a trail following the old railway route — allow a relaxed half-day there.

faq.q: What are the must-see attractions in Kanchanaburi?
faq.a: For a first visit, start with the Bridge over the River Kwai, Erawan Falls, and Wat Tham Suea — the most well-known and easiest to reach. With more time, extend to Mon Bridge in Sangkhlaburi and Hellfire Pass Museum in Sai Yok.

faq.q: What are the highlights of Kanchanaburi?
faq.a: The standouts are Erawan Falls — a 7-tier limestone waterfall with emerald-green water inside Erawan National Park — and the Bridge over the River Kwai, which still has the historic train running across it every day. For nature and cultural depth, Mon Bridge in Sangkhlaburi is famous for winter-morning mist rolling over the water.

faq.q: Are entry fees expensive in Kanchanaburi?
faq.a: Most major landmarks — the Bridge over the River Kwai, Wat Tham Suea, the Giant Chamchuri Tree, and Mon Bridge — are free to enter. Erawan Falls charges 60 THB for Thai adults and 300 THB for foreigners, plus 30 THB for vehicles. Song Khwae Skywalk is around 60 THB. Hellfire Pass Museum is free.

faq.q: Is it easy to get around and park in Kanchanaburi?
faq.a: Driving your own car or renting one is the recommended approach, since attractions are spread out and public transport options are limited. Several landmarks have free parking — the Giant Chamchuri Tree and Wat Tham Suea both do. Erawan Falls and Sangkhlaburi are far from town; budget extra time and fuel.

faq.q: What time do Kanchanaburi attractions open?
faq.a: The national park and nature sites like Erawan Falls have daytime hours and stop admitting visitors to upper tiers before closing — going early is essential. Wat Tham Suea opens from around 7 AM. Hellfire Pass Museum opens approximately 09:00–16:00. Ploen Kan Market and the Pak Phraek riverfront walking street are evening venues that open from late afternoon into the night.
